points: Solute dissolves, solvent does the dissolving, solution is the even mixture.
Concentration is a ratio: amount of solute per amount of solution.
Dilution adds solvent and lowers concentration; solute mass stays the same.
Concentration (g/L) = mass of solute / volume of solution.
Solubility is the maximum that dissolves; it depends on temperature.

faqs.q: What is the difference between solute, solvent, and solution?
faqs.a: The solute is the substance that dissolves, the solvent is the substance it dissolves in, and the solution is the uniform mixture that results. In sugary tea, sugar is the solute, water is the solvent, and the sweet tea is the solution.

faqs.q: How do I calculate concentration in g/L?
faqs.a: Divide the mass of solute in grams by the volume of the whole solution in litres: concentration = mass / volume. For example, 15 g in 0.5 L gives 30 g/L.

faqs.q: What happens to concentration when I dilute a solution?
faqs.a: The concentration falls because the same mass of solute is spread through more solvent. If the volume doubles, the concentration halves; if it increases five times, the concentration drops to one-fifth.

faqs.q: What is a saturated solution?
faqs.a: A solution holding the maximum amount of solute that will dissolve at that temperature. Adding more solute leaves it undissolved at the bottom.

faqs.q: Does temperature affect solubility?
faqs.a: Yes. Most solids dissolve better in hot water than in cold. Gases do the opposite — they dissolve better in cold water, which is why a warm fizzy drink goes flat quickly.

title: Motion, Speed and Velocity: What Is the Difference?
desc: Race and rickshaw examples separate distance, displacement, speed, and velocity so pupils can use each word correctly in physics.
intro:
When a rickshaw travels from your home to school, everyone says it is moving, but physics asks two sharper questions: how far did it travel, and in which direction did it end up? Motion means a change of position with time, and the words we use to describe motion are not interchangeable. Distance tells you the total length of the path, while displacement tells you the straight-line change from the starting point to the finishing point, together with its direction. Speed tells you how fast something moves, while velocity tells you how fast it moves and in which direction. Mixing these words up is one of the most common mistakes in physics, and this article clears it up with races, rickshaw journeys, and walks around the school ground.

By the end of this article you will be able to look at any journey and say four things about it: the distance covered, the displacement, the average speed, and the average velocity. You will also know why a runner who completes one full lap of a track can have a large distance but zero displacement, and why a car driving steadily around a roundabout is changing its velocity even when its speedometer does not move. These ideas are the foundation of every later topic in mechanics, so it is worth getting them exactly right now. Keep your physics notebook open and sketch each example as you read, because drawing the path is the fastest way to see the difference.

paras: An object is in motion when its position changes relative to a fixed reference point as time passes. A book sitting on your desk is at rest relative to the desk, but the same book is moving relative to the Sun, because the Earth carries it along. That is why physics always asks: motion relative to what? In school problems, the reference point is usually the ground, a starting line, or your home, and you measure positions from there. If the position does not change, the object is at rest; if it changes, the object is in motion.

Motion can be described in three simple ways: by the path taken, by how fast the position changes, and by whether the direction changes. A ball rolling down a straight slope, a swing moving back and forth, and a bicycle going around a bend are all in motion, but their paths look different. Before doing any calculation, form the habit of naming the path: straight line, curved, or back-and-forth. That one habit prevents many errors, because the formulas for distance and displacement behave differently on a curved or return journey. You can practise this habit with the everyday examples in [force and motion in daily life](/blog/science-force-motion-daily-examples.html).

sections.h2: Distance: The Full Length of the Journey
paras: Distance is the total length of the path an object actually travels. It is a scalar quantity, which means it has size but no direction. If a rickshaw leaves home, travels 3 kilometres east to the market, then 2 kilometres north to school, the distance is 5 kilometres, because you add every part of the journey. The odometer in a vehicle measures distance: it keeps adding up every metre the wheels turn, no matter which way the vehicle turns. Distance is never negative, and it never decreases as a journey goes on.

A useful way to remember distance is to think of a piece of string laid along the exact route. Straighten the string and measure it, and you have the distance. A pupil who walks from the classroom to the canteen and back has covered twice the one-way distance, even though the pupil ends up back in the classroom. In word problems, look for phrases like total path, how far, or length of the journey. Those phrases almost always mean distance. When you calculate it, add each leg of the journey carefully, and keep the unit the same throughout, usually metres or kilometres.

sections.h2: Displacement: From Start to Finish in a Straight Line
paras: Displacement is the change in position from the starting point to the finishing point, measured in a straight line, together with the direction. It is a vector quantity, which means it has both size and direction. In the rickshaw example above, the displacement is not 5 kilometres; it is the straight line from home to school, which is shorter than the travelled path, and it points in the direction from home to school. If you walk around the whole school ground and return to your starting point, your displacement is zero, because your finishing position is exactly your starting position, even though your legs are tired from walking a real distance.

This is the idea that confuses most pupils, so practise it with drawings. Draw a dot for the start and a dot for the finish, then join them with a straight arrow. That arrow is the displacement. The length of the arrow is the size, and the arrowhead shows the direction. In a race, two runners can cover the same distance but have different displacements if they finish at different places. And a runner who starts and finishes at the same line after one full lap has a displacement of zero. If a question asks how far an object is from its starting point, or asks for the change in position, it is asking about displacement. Sketching the path is the skill that turns these questions easy, and the same drawing habit helps with [diagrams and labelling](/blog/science-diagrams-labelling-habits.html).

diagram.alt: Distance vs Displacement on the Same Journey
diagram.caption: One journey, two measures: distance follows the path, displacement joins start to finish.

paras: Speed is the distance covered divided by the time taken. Its unit is metres per second (m/s) or kilometres per hour (km/h). If a pupil walks 100 metres in 50 seconds, the average speed is 2 m/s. Notice the word average: during the walk, the pupil may have walked faster at the start and slower at the end, but the average speed describes the whole journey in one number. The speedometer of a car shows the speed at one instant, called instantaneous speed, while dividing the total distance by the total time gives the average speed for the whole trip.

Speed problems become easy when you write the formula in words first: speed equals distance divided by time. Then write the numbers with units, and only then calculate. A common mistake is to mix units, for example dividing kilometres by seconds. Convert everything to one pair of units before you calculate: either metres and seconds, or kilometres and hours. To convert km/h to m/s, multiply by 5/18; to convert m/s to km/h, multiply by 18/5. Practise with real journeys you know: time your walk to school, estimate the distance, and find your average speed. Numbers that come from your own life are remembered far better than numbers from a page.

Velocity is the displacement divided by the time taken, and it includes direction. If a car travels 60 kilometres east in one hour, its velocity is 60 km/h east. If the same car turns around and travels 60 kilometres west in one hour, its speed is the same, but its velocity has changed completely, because the direction is opposite. This is why velocity is a vector and speed is a scalar. In everyday speech people say velocity when they mean speed, but in physics the direction is part of the meaning.

The most important consequence is this: an object moving at constant speed can still be changing its velocity if its direction changes. A bicycle going steadily around a circular track has a constant speed, but its velocity changes at every moment because its direction keeps changing. That changing velocity means the bicycle is accelerating, even though the speedometer reading stays the same. Examiners love this idea, so learn it as a sentence you can write from memory: constant speed in a circle means changing velocity, because velocity includes direction. The same careful reading of direction helps with [physics numerical problems](/blog/class-12-physics-numerical-problem-approach.html).

A second useful case is the return journey. If you walk 400 metres east to a shop in 5 minutes and walk back 400 metres west in 5 minutes, your total distance is 800 metres and your average speed is 80 metres per minute. But your displacement for the whole trip is zero, because you finished where you started, so your average velocity for the whole trip is zero. The two answers look strange side by side, yet both are correct, because they measure different things. Whenever a question seems to have a trick, check whether it is asking about distance or displacement.

sections.h2: A Five-Step Method for Motion Problems
paras: Use this method on every motion question, and your marks will rise. First, read the question twice and underline the words that tell you whether it wants distance or displacement, speed or velocity. Second, draw the path: a dot for the start, arrows for each leg, and a dot for the finish. Third, write the formula in words before you touch numbers. Fourth, convert all units to one consistent pair. Fifth, check the answer by asking whether it is sensible: is the distance at least as big as the displacement? Is the speed reasonable for a person, a bicycle, or a car? A walking speed of 200 m/s is impossible, so a result like that means a unit error.

Practise with three journeys from your own day: the walk from home to school, one lap of the school ground, and a rickshaw ride with one turn. For each journey, write down the distance, the displacement, the time, the average speed, and the average velocity with direction. Three worked examples of your own are worth more than twenty copied ones, because you know the routes and can picture every turn. If you get stuck, re-read the compare diagram in this article and ask which column your question belongs to. Solved notes and class material are listed on the [solved notes page](/solved.html).

diagram.alt: Solving Any Motion Question in Five Steps
diagram.caption: Follow the steps in order; do not calculate before you have drawn the path.

points: Distance is the total path length; displacement is the straight-line change from start to finish with direction.
Speed is distance divided by time and has no direction; velocity is displacement divided by time and includes direction.
A full lap of a track gives a large distance but zero displacement.
Constant speed in a circle means changing velocity, because the direction keeps changing.
Draw the path before calculating, and keep units consistent throughout.

faqs.q: What is the difference between distance and displacement?
faqs.a: Distance is the total length of the path travelled, with no direction. Displacement is the straight-line change from the starting point to the finishing point, with direction. Distance is always at least as large as the size of the displacement, and displacement can be zero even after a long journey, for example one full lap of a track.

faqs.q: Can velocity be zero while speed is not zero?
faqs.a: Yes. On a return journey, the average velocity over the whole trip is zero because the displacement is zero, but the average speed is positive because distance was covered. Instantaneous velocity can also be zero at the turning point of a swing, even though the object was moving a moment before.

faqs.q: How do I convert km/h to m/s?
faqs.a: Multiply the km/h value by 5/18. For example, 72 km/h becomes 72 x 5/18 = 20 m/s. To convert the other way, multiply an m/s value by 18/5. Always convert units before calculating so distance and time use one consistent pair.

faqs.q: Why does a car going steadily around a roundabout have changing velocity?
faqs.a: Velocity includes direction. Around a roundabout the car's speed may stay steady, but its direction changes at every moment, so its velocity changes too. A changing velocity means the car is accelerating, even though the speedometer reading does not move.

faqs.q: What is the most common mistake in motion problems?
faqs.a: Using distance where the question asks for displacement, or speed where it asks for velocity. Underline the key words in the question, draw the path, and check whether direction matters before you calculate.

title: Newton's Laws of Motion with Everyday Examples
desc: Each of Newton's three laws is explained through cricket, cycling, and seat-belt examples that pupils already know from daily life.
intro:
When a batsman hits a cricket ball, when a cyclist stops pedalling, and when a car brakes suddenly, the same three rules are at work. Newton's laws of motion describe how forces change the motion of objects, and they explain things you see every day. The first law says that an object keeps its state of motion unless a force acts on it. The second law says that a force produces acceleration, and that a bigger force or a smaller mass gives a bigger acceleration. The third law says that forces always come in pairs: for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.

These laws sound abstract when they are written in one line, but they become obvious once you attach them to things you already know. This article takes each law in turn and explains it with cricket, cycling, seat belts, and other everyday scenes from life in Pakistan. You will also learn the common mistakes pupils make with each law, and how to answer exam questions that ask you to identify which law is acting in a given situation. By the end, you will be able to watch any moving object and name the law behind what it does.

paras: A force is a push or a pull that can change the motion of an object. It can start a stationary object moving, stop a moving object, change its speed, change its direction, or change its shape. Forces are measured in newtons (N), named after Isaac Newton. When you push a desk, kick a ball, or stretch a rubber band, you apply a force. Some forces need contact, like friction and the push of your hand. Others act at a distance, like gravity pulling an apple down and magnetism pulling a nail toward a magnet.

Forces are vectors: they have size and direction. Two forces can add up or cancel out depending on their directions. If two pupils push a desk in the same direction, the pushes add. If they push in opposite directions with equal strength, the desk does not move, because the forces balance. This idea of balanced and unbalanced forces is the key to the first law. When the forces on an object are balanced, its motion does not change; when they are unbalanced, its motion changes. Many pupils think a force is needed to keep an object moving, but as the first law shows, that is not true. Class physics material is listed on the [books page](/books.html).

sections.h2: First Law: Objects Keep Their Motion
paras: Newton's first law, the law of inertia, says that an object remains at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless an unbalanced force acts on it. Inertia is the resistance of an object to a change in its motion. A heavy object has more inertia than a light one, which is why a loaded school bag is harder to start moving and harder to stop than an empty one. On a perfectly smooth surface with no friction, a sliding object would keep sliding forever, because nothing would act to slow it down.

Everyday life is full of inertia. When a bus starts suddenly, passengers lurch backward, because their bodies tend to stay at rest while the bus moves forward. When the bus brakes suddenly, passengers lurch forward, because their bodies tend to keep moving while the bus slows down. That is why seat belts matter: the belt provides the unbalanced force that stops your body with the car instead of letting it continue forward. A cricket ball rolling on the ground slows down because friction provides an unbalanced force, not because motion needs a force to continue. The dusting of a carpet by beating it, the way a coin drops into a glass when a card is flicked away, and the way a tablecloth can be pulled from under dishes are all first-law demonstrations. If a question describes something continuing as it was until something forces a change, it is testing the first law.

The first law also explains why you should wear a helmet on a bicycle. If the bicycle stops suddenly against an obstacle, your body keeps moving forward, and the helmet protects the part of you most at risk. Inertia is not a force pushing you; it is your body's tendency to keep its motion. Remembering that distinction will save you from one of the most common wrong answers in physics.

sections.h2: Second Law: Force, Mass and Acceleration
paras: Newton's second law says that the acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the net force acting on it and inversely proportional to its mass. In symbols: F = ma, force equals mass times acceleration. The same force gives a small acceleration to a heavy object and a large acceleration to a light one. Push an empty shopping cart and a full one with the same effort, and the empty one speeds up much faster. That is the second law in action.

Cricket gives a clear example. A fast bowler's delivery reaches the batsman with a certain speed. If the batsman stops the ball quickly, in a short time, the force on the bat is large. If the batsman lets the ball travel with the bat, slowing it over a longer time, the force is smaller. Fielders use the same idea when they pull their hands back as they catch a fast ball: lengthening the time of the catch reduces the force on their hands. The law can also be read the other way: to give a heavy object the same acceleration as a light one, you need a bigger force. That is why pushing a loaded truck takes far more effort than pushing a bicycle.

When you solve second-law problems, follow this routine: list the mass in kilograms, the acceleration in metres per second squared, and the net force in newtons. Write F = ma, substitute the numbers with units, and calculate. Watch out for weight, which is a force: weight equals mass times the acceleration due to gravity (W = mg). A 10 kg bag has a weight of about 98 N, but its mass is still 10 kg. Mixing up mass and weight is the most common second-law mistake, so always check which one the question gives you. The method of working carefully through numbers also helps with [physics numerical problems](/blog/class-12-physics-numerical-problem-approach.html).

diagram.alt: Using F = ma Without Mixing Up Mass and Weight
diagram.caption: Work in kilograms, metres per second squared, and newtons.

sections.h2: Third Law: Every Action Has a Reaction
paras: Newton's third law says that for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. When one object exerts a force on a second object, the second object exerts an equal force in the opposite direction on the first. The two forces act on different objects, which is the detail most pupils forget. If the two forces acted on the same object, they would cancel and nothing would ever move, but they act on different objects, so motion happens.

Walking is a third-law act. Your foot pushes backward on the ground, and the ground pushes forward on your foot, moving you ahead. A swimmer pushes water backward and the water pushes the swimmer forward. A rocket pushes hot gases downward and the gases push the rocket upward. A cricket bat hits a ball forward, and the ball pushes back on the bat, which is why a hard hit stings the hands. A bird flies because its wings push air downward and the air pushes the wings upward. In each case, the pair of forces is equal in size and opposite in direction, but they act on different bodies.

A famous trap question asks: if the action and reaction are equal and opposite, why does anything move? The answer is that the two forces act on different objects. The action of the horse on the cart and the reaction of the cart on the horse are equal, but the cart still moves because the net force on the cart is forward. When you answer third-law questions, always name both objects and both forces: object A pushes object B, and object B pushes object A. Naming the pair in full is what earns full marks.

sections.h2: Which Law Is This? A Quick Test
paras: Exam questions often describe a situation and ask which law it shows. Use these clues. If something keeps its motion until a force changes it, or if the question mentions inertia, a seat belt, or a sudden stop, it is the first law. If the question gives a force, a mass, and an acceleration, or asks how one of them changes when another changes, it is the second law. If the question describes two objects pushing each other, or a pair of forces in opposite directions, it is the third law. Many questions combine laws, so read carefully: a rocket accelerating uses the third law to produce thrust and the second law to relate that thrust to its acceleration.

Try this test on three scenes. A cyclist stops pedalling and slowly comes to rest: the first law, because friction is the unbalanced force that changes the motion. A batsman hits a ball and it accelerates off the bat: the second law, because the force of the bat produces the ball's acceleration, and the third law, because the ball pushes back on the bat. A balloon flies when its air escapes: the third law, because the air rushes one way and the balloon moves the other. Practise naming the law for ten scenes a day for a week, and the identification skill becomes automatic. Related everyday physics is covered in [force and motion in daily life](/blog/science-force-motion-daily-examples.html).

diagram.alt: The Three Laws at a Glance
diagram.caption: One map for all three laws: inertia, F = ma, and action-reaction.

points: First law: an object keeps its motion unless an unbalanced force acts on it; this resistance is inertia.
Second law: F = ma — acceleration grows with force and shrinks with mass.
Third law: forces come in equal, opposite pairs acting on different objects.
Seat belts work by providing the unbalanced force that stops your body with the car.
Name both objects and both forces when answering third-law questions.

faqs.q: Why do passengers lurch forward when a bus brakes suddenly?
faqs.a: Because of inertia, from the first law. The passengers' bodies tend to keep moving forward while the bus slows down. The seat or a seat belt provides the unbalanced force that slows the passengers with the bus.

faqs.q: What is the difference between mass and weight in F = ma?
faqs.a: Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms, and it does not change with location. Weight is the force of gravity on that mass, W = mg, measured in newtons. In F = ma, m is the mass, never the weight.

faqs.q: If action and reaction are equal, why does anything move?
faqs.a: Because the two forces act on different objects. When you walk, your foot pushes the ground backward and the ground pushes you forward. The force on you is unbalanced, so you move, even though the pair of forces is equal and opposite.

faqs.q: Why do fielders pull their hands back when catching a fast ball?
faqs.a: Pulling the hands back lengthens the time over which the ball slows down, which reduces the force on the hands. This follows from the second law: the same change in motion spread over more time needs a smaller force.

faqs.q: How can I tell which law a question is testing?
faqs.a: Keeping motion or inertia points to the first law; force, mass, and acceleration point to the second; two objects pushing each other points to the third. Name the clue words in the question before you choose.

title: Work, Energy and Power in Physics: Clear Meanings
desc: Everyday and physics meanings of work are separated with lifting, climbing, and cycling examples pupils can picture and calculate.
intro:
In everyday speech, you work when you study, when you write homework, and when you hold a heavy bag. In physics, work, energy, and power have much narrower meanings: work is done only when a force moves an object in the direction of the force. Holding a heavy bag still, however tiring it feels, is not work in the physics sense, because nothing moves. This difference between the everyday word and the physics word confuses many pupils, and it is the first thing to clear up.

This article separates the three ideas cleanly: work, energy, and power. Work is energy transferred by a force acting through a distance. Energy is the capacity to do work, and it appears in many forms, such as kinetic energy, potential energy, heat, and chemical energy. Power is how quickly work is done or energy is transferred. You will meet each idea through lifting, climbing stairs, and cycling, and you will learn the formulas with the correct units so that you can use them in numerical problems without mixing them up.

sections.h2: Work in Physics: Force Times Distance
paras: Work is calculated as force multiplied by the distance moved in the direction of the force: W = F x d. Its unit is the joule (J), which is one newton-metre. If you push a box with a force of 50 N and it moves 4 metres in the direction of the push, you do 200 J of work. If the same push moves nothing, the work done is zero, no matter how hard you push. That is the rule that separates physics work from everyday effort.

Direction matters. Only the part of the force that acts along the direction of motion counts. If you pull a suitcase with a strap angled upward, only the horizontal part of your pull does work in moving it forward; the upward part holds some of its weight. And if you carry a bag horizontally across a room, gravity does no work on the bag, because the bag does not move in the direction of gravity. This is why a porter carrying luggage across a flat platform does no work against gravity, even though the porter feels tired: the muscles work to hold the load, but the load does not move vertically. In exam questions, always ask two things: did something move, and was the force along that movement?

sections.h2: Why Holding a Bag Is Not Physics Work
paras: This is the classic trap, so it deserves its own section. A pupil holding a 10 kg bag still at shoulder height feels the effort in the arms, and the muscles burn energy, so it seems obvious that work is being done. But the bag does not move, so the distance in W = F x d is zero, and the work done on the bag is zero. The tiredness comes from biology: muscles consume energy to maintain tension even without movement. Physics does not deny the tiredness; it simply uses the word work for something narrower.

Compare three cases to fix the idea. A pupil lifting a bag from the floor to a table does work, because the force acts upward and the bag moves upward. A pupil holding the bag still on the table does no work, because there is no movement. A pupil carrying the bag horizontally at steady height does no work against gravity, because the movement is sideways while gravity pulls downward. If an exam question asks about work done by gravity, or work done by a porter, or work done by a waiter, draw the force arrow and the movement arrow, and check whether they point in the same direction. That one sketch answers the question. Solved notes and class material are listed on the [solved notes page](/solved.html) and the [books page](/books.html).

diagram.alt: Work Done vs No Work Done
diagram.caption: Same effort can mean work in one case and no work in another.

sections.h2: Energy: The Capacity to Do Work
paras: Energy is the capacity to do work, and it is measured in joules, the same unit as work. Energy appears in many forms and changes from one form to another, but it is never created or destroyed. This is the law of conservation of energy. A moving cricket ball has kinetic energy, the energy of motion. A ball held high above the ground has gravitational potential energy, the energy of position. A stretched rubber band has elastic potential energy. Food has chemical energy, a battery stores chemical energy, and a hot cup of tea has thermal energy.

The two mechanical forms are the ones you will calculate most. Kinetic energy is KE = 1/2 mv squared, where m is mass and v is speed. A fast, heavy object has much more kinetic energy than a slow, light one, because the speed is squared: doubling the speed multiplies the kinetic energy by four. Gravitational potential energy is PE = mgh, where m is mass, g is the acceleration due to gravity, and h is height. Lifting a bag higher, or lifting a heavier bag, gives it more potential energy. When the bag falls, that potential energy changes into kinetic energy, and just before it lands, almost all of it is kinetic. Tracing these changes is the heart of energy questions.

Watch a child on a swing to see energy change in real time. At the highest point, the swing moves slowly and has maximum potential energy and minimum kinetic energy. At the lowest point, it moves fastest and has maximum kinetic energy and minimum potential energy. As the swing rises again, kinetic energy changes back into potential energy. The total energy stays the same, apart from a small amount lost to air resistance and friction as heat, which is why a swing gradually slows unless someone pushes it.

A cyclist riding down a hill shows the same pattern. At the top, the cyclist has potential energy. Rolling down, potential energy changes into kinetic energy, and the cyclist speeds up. A hydroelectric dam uses the same idea on a huge scale: water stored high behind the dam has potential energy, falling water gains kinetic energy, and turbines change that kinetic energy into electrical energy. In your own home, a torch changes chemical energy in the battery into electrical energy and then into light and heat. When you answer energy questions, name the starting form, the change, and the final form, in that order. That three-part sentence is what examiners look for.

sections.h2: Power: How Fast Work Is Done
paras: Power is the rate of doing work, or the rate of transferring energy: P = W / t. Its unit is the watt (W), which is one joule per second. Two pupils can lift the same bags up the same stairs, doing the same work, but the pupil who finishes in half the time has twice the power. Power is about speed of work, not amount of work. A powerful car engine is one that can convert fuel energy into motion quickly, and a powerful bulb is one that converts electrical energy into light and heat quickly.

Everyday power ratings are a good way to practise. A 100 W bulb uses 100 joules of electrical energy every second. A 60 W bulb uses less energy per second and is dimmer. An electric motor rated 1000 W can do 1000 joules of work every second. When you see horsepower, remember that one horsepower is about 746 watts. In numerical problems, the common trap is to confuse energy and power: energy is the total amount, in joules, while power is the rate, in watts. If a question asks how much energy is used in 10 seconds, multiply power by time. If it asks for power, divide the work by the time. The [solved notes page](/solved.html) lists class material where these formulas are practised.

Climbing stairs is the best self-test. Weigh yourself in kilograms, measure the height of one flight of stairs in metres, count the steps, and time your climb. Your work is mgh, and your power is that work divided by the time. A pupil who climbs faster produces more power even though the work is the same. Try it twice, once slowly and once quickly, and the meaning of power becomes physical, not just a formula.

sections.h2: Solving Work, Energy and Power Problems
paras: Use a fixed routine. First, identify which quantity the question asks for: work (joules), energy (joules), or power (watts). Second, write the formula in words and symbols. Third, convert units: mass to kilograms, distance to metres, time to seconds. Fourth, substitute and calculate. Fifth, check the unit of your answer: joules for work and energy, watts for power. If your power answer comes out in joules, you have divided the wrong way or forgotten the time.

Watch for three traps. Trap one: mass given in grams must be converted to kilograms before using KE or PE. Trap two: speed must be squared in kinetic energy, so a small error in speed becomes a large error in energy. Trap three: height in potential energy is the vertical height, not the length of a slope. A pupil pushed up a ramp 10 metres long but only 2 metres high gains mgh with h = 2 m, not 10 m. Drawing the height as a vertical arrow beside the slope prevents this mistake. A careful, labelled sketch is worth more than a memorised formula, as the same habit helps with [diagrams and labelling](/blog/science-diagrams-labelling-habits.html).

diagram.caption: Ask which quantity the question wants before you write anything.

points: Work is done only when a force moves an object in the direction of the force: W = F x d, in joules.
Holding a heavy bag still is not work in physics, because the distance moved is zero.
Energy is the capacity to do work; it changes form but is never created or destroyed.
Kinetic energy is 1/2 mv squared; gravitational potential energy is mgh with vertical height.
Power is the rate of doing work: P = W / t, in watts; faster work means more power.

faqs.q: Is holding a heavy bag work in physics?
faqs.a: No. The bag does not move, so the distance in W = F x d is zero and the work done on the bag is zero. Your muscles still use energy to maintain tension, which is why you feel tired, but physics reserves the word work for a force acting through a distance.

faqs.q: What is the difference between energy and power?
faqs.a: Energy is the total capacity to do work, measured in joules. Power is how quickly that energy is transferred or work is done, measured in watts (joules per second). The same work done in half the time means twice the power.

faqs.q: Why is speed squared in kinetic energy?
faqs.a: Because KE = 1/2 mv squared. Doubling the speed multiplies the kinetic energy by four, and tripling it multiplies the energy by nine. That is why a small increase in the speed of a vehicle makes a crash much more severe.

faqs.q: In PE = mgh, is h the length of the slope or the vertical height?
faqs.a: The vertical height only. A pupil pushed up a ramp 10 metres long but only 2 metres high gains potential energy mgh with h = 2 m. Drawing the height as a vertical arrow beside the slope prevents this common mistake.

faqs.q: What is one watt?
faqs.a: One watt is one joule of work done, or one joule of energy transferred, every second. A 100 W bulb uses 100 joules of electrical energy per second. Power in watts equals work in joules divided by time in seconds.

title: Pressure in Liquids and Gases, Explained Simply
desc: Syringes, balloons, and water tanks show how pressure spreads, grows with depth, and changes when area or force changes.
intro:
Pressure in liquids and gases is still force spread over an area. The same force feels very different depending on the area it acts on: a sharp pin hurts because its force is concentrated on a tiny point, while the same push spread across your whole palm feels gentle. In physics, pressure equals force divided by area, P = F / A, and its unit is the pascal (Pa), which is one newton per square metre. This one idea explains why wide tyres grip soft ground, why a sharp knife cuts, and why a dam wall is thicker at the bottom than at the top.

Liquids and gases, called fluids, add two more ideas: pressure in a liquid grows with depth, and pressure acts in all directions. This article builds the idea of pressure step by step with syringes, balloons, and water tanks that you can picture or safely try with an adult's supervision. You will learn why pressure in a liquid depends on depth and density but not on the shape of the container, how a small force on a small piston can lift a heavy car, and why atmospheric pressure, the weight of the air above us, matters to everything from drinking through a straw to weather.

paras: Pressure is defined as force divided by the area over which the force acts: P = F / A. The unit is the pascal (Pa). If you press with a force of 100 N on an area of 1 square metre, the pressure is 100 Pa. Press with the same force on an area of 0.01 square metres, and the pressure becomes 10,000 Pa, one hundred times greater. That is why a pointed nail goes into wood with a small push, while the flat head of the same nail would need a hammer blow to move at all.

Everyday life gives many examples. Snow shoes spread a person's weight over a wide area so the pressure is low and the wearer does not sink into snow. A tractor has wide tyres for the same reason: low pressure on soft soil. A sharp kitchen knife cuts because the force of your hand is concentrated along a thin edge. A school bag with wide straps feels lighter than the same bag with narrow straps, because the wide straps spread the weight over a larger area of your shoulder. Whenever a question asks why something is sharp, wide, or pointed, the answer almost always comes back to pressure equals force over area. Keep a notebook list of such examples from your own home and school, because they make the best exam answers.

sections.h2: Pressure in Liquids Grows With Depth
paras: In a liquid, pressure increases with depth. The deeper you go, the more liquid sits above you, and the weight of that liquid presses down. That is why your ears feel the pressure when you dive to the bottom of a deep pool, and why a dam wall is built thickest at the bottom, where the water pressure is greatest. The pressure at a depth h in a liquid is given by P = h x rho x g, where rho is the density of the liquid and g is the acceleration due to gravity. So pressure grows with depth, with the density of the liquid, and it does not depend on the shape of the container.

A simple picture proves the shape point. Imagine three containers holding water to the same depth: a narrow tube, a wide tank, and a cone-shaped vessel. The pressure at the bottom is the same in all three, because the depth is the same, even though the amounts of water are very different. Pupils often guess that the container with more water has more pressure, but pressure depends on depth, not on total volume. You can see this with a plastic bottle: make small holes at different heights with an adult's help, fill the bottle, and watch the water from the lowest hole travel farthest, because the pressure there is greatest. The top hole dribbles, because the pressure near the surface is smallest.

diagram.alt: Why a Dam Wall Is Thickest at the Bottom
diagram.caption: Water pressure grows with depth, so the bottom of the wall carries the greatest push.

paras: Pressure in a fluid pushes in every direction, not only downward. The water at the bottom of a tank pushes down on the floor, sideways on the walls, and upward on anything floating in it. A balloon inflates into a sphere because the air inside pushes equally in all directions. A punctured bicycle tube leaks from any point because the air pressure pushes outward everywhere, not just at the bottom.

This all-directions property explains the syringe. When you block the nozzle of a syringe and push the plunger, the air inside is compressed, and its pressure rises and pushes back against the plunger in every direction. Release the plunger and the compressed air pushes it back out. A hydraulic jack uses the same idea in a cleverer way: pressure applied to a small piston is transmitted through the liquid to a large piston, and because the large piston has a much bigger area, the force on it is much bigger. A small push can therefore lift a heavy car. This is Pascal's law: pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished to every part of the fluid. Brakes in cars and buses work on the same principle.

Air is a fluid too, so it has pressure. Atmospheric pressure is the weight of the whole column of air above us pressing down. At sea level it is about 101,300 Pa, roughly the weight of ten tonnes on every square metre. We do not feel crushed because the air inside our bodies pushes outward with the same pressure. When you drink through a straw, you do not pull the drink up by suction: you remove some air from the straw, the atmospheric pressure on the surface of the drink pushes the liquid up into the low-pressure straw, and the drink rises.

Gas pressure changes when you change the volume or the temperature. Squeezing a gas into a smaller volume raises its pressure, which is why a bicycle pump gets hard to push as the tyre fills. Heating a sealed gas raises its pressure, which is why spray cans warn against heat: the pressure can rise until the can bursts. This is a safety rule, not just physics: never heat a sealed container, and never puncture a spray can. A balloon left in the sun expands because the air inside gets warmer and its pressure rises. Weather forecasters measure air pressure with a barometer: falling pressure often means a storm is coming, because air is rising and cooling.

Pressure is measured with gauges and barometers. A tyre pressure gauge reads the pressure inside the tyre, usually in psi or kilopascals. A barometer measures atmospheric pressure, and a manometer compares the pressure of a gas with the atmosphere. In school work, you will mostly calculate with P = F / A and P = h x rho x g, and you must keep units consistent: force in newtons, area in square metres, depth in metres, density in kilograms per cubic metre. A common error is to use area in square centimetres; convert to square metres first by dividing by 10,000.

Pressure ideas also protect you in daily life. Check that a pressure cooker valve is clear before use, because a blocked valve lets pressure build dangerously. Do not over-inflate a bicycle tyre or a balloon beyond its rated pressure. When you use a syringe for a school demonstration, do it only with a teacher's permission and never point it at anyone. The physics of pressure is powerful precisely because a small change in area or depth can produce a large change in force, so treat pressure experiments with the same care you would give any experiment. Good experiment habits are covered in [writing up a science experiment](/blog/science-experiment-write-up-observation.html). More class material is on the [books page](/books.html) and the [blog index](/blog/).

points: Pressure is force divided by area: P = F / A, measured in pascals.
Pressure in a liquid grows with depth and density, not with the shape of the container.
Fluid pressure acts in all directions, which is why balloons inflate evenly.
Pascal's law lets a small force on a small piston produce a large force on a large piston.
Atmospheric pressure is the weight of the air above us; drinking through a straw uses it.

faqs.q: Why is a dam wall thicker at the bottom?
faqs.a: Because water pressure increases with depth. The bottom of the wall carries the weight of the deepest water, so it faces the greatest pressure and must be built thickest. Pressure at a depth is P = h x rho x g.

faqs.q: Does the shape of a container change the pressure at the bottom?
faqs.a: No, if the depth is the same. A narrow tube, a wide tank, and a cone-shaped vessel filled to the same depth all have the same pressure at the bottom. Pressure depends on depth and density, not on total volume or container shape.

faqs.q: How does a hydraulic jack lift a heavy car with a small push?
faqs.a: By Pascal's law: pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted to every part. A small force on a small piston creates a pressure that acts on a large piston with a much bigger area, producing a much bigger force.

faqs.q: Why does drinking through a straw work?
faqs.a: When you suck, you lower the air pressure inside the straw. Atmospheric pressure pushing on the surface of the drink is then greater than the pressure in the straw, so it pushes the liquid up into the straw and into your mouth.

faqs.q: Why should you never heat a sealed spray can?
faqs.a: Heating a sealed gas raises its pressure. In a spray can the pressure can rise until the can bursts, which is dangerous. Always keep sealed cans away from heat and never puncture them.

title: Light: Reflection and Refraction with Ray Diagrams
desc: Ray diagrams pupils can reproduce trace light through mirrors and water, showing reflection and refraction step by step.
intro:
Light travels in straight lines, and that single fact explains mirrors, lenses, rainbows, and why a straw in a glass of water looks bent. When light meets a surface, it can bounce back, which is reflection, or it can pass into a new material and change direction, which is refraction. Both behaviours follow simple rules, and both are best learned by drawing ray diagrams: straight lines with arrowheads showing where the light goes. A pupil who can draw the ray diagram can answer almost any question about light.

This article teaches you to draw those diagrams yourself. You will learn the law of reflection with a plane mirror, how images form in mirrors, and why a spoon in water looks broken at the surface. You will practise with mirrors and a glass of water at home, using safe, simple observations. By the end, you will be able to trace rays through a mirror and through water, label the angles, and explain what you see in your own words. The [solved notes page](/solved.html) lists class material where these diagrams appear. More science material is on the [books page](/books.html) and the [blog index](/blog/).

paras: A ray is a straight line showing the path of light, and a beam is a group of rays. Shadows are the simplest proof that light travels straight: an object blocks the rays, and the shadow is the region the rays cannot reach. A pinhole camera works the same way: light from each point of an object passes through a tiny hole in a straight line and forms an upside-down image on the screen. The image is upside down because rays from the top of the object travel downward through the hole, and rays from the bottom travel upward.

This straight-line rule is the foundation of every ray diagram. When you draw a diagram, use a ruler for every ray, add an arrowhead to show the direction of travel, and label the important lines: the incident ray coming in, the reflected or refracted ray going out, and the normal, a line drawn at right angles to the surface at the point where the ray meets it. Angles in optics are always measured from the normal, never from the surface. That one rule, angles from the normal, prevents more mistakes than any other single habit in this topic.

sections.h2: Reflection: The Law of the Mirror
paras: When light hits a smooth surface like a mirror, it reflects. The law of reflection says that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and that the incident ray, the reflected ray, and the normal all lie in the same plane. The angle of incidence is the angle between the incoming ray and the normal; the angle of reflection is the angle between the outgoing ray and the normal. If a ray strikes a mirror at 30 degrees to the normal, it leaves at 30 degrees to the normal, on the other side.

A plane mirror forms an image that is upright, the same size as the object, and as far behind the mirror as the object is in front of it. The image is virtual, which means the light rays do not actually meet behind the mirror; your brain follows the reflected rays backward and sees the image there. It is also laterally inverted, so writing appears back to front. A periscope uses two mirrors at 45 degrees to let you see over an obstacle, and the mirrors in a barber's shop use two reflections to show the back of your head. To draw a plane-mirror diagram, draw the mirror, place the object, draw two rays from one point of the object to the mirror, reflect each with equal angles, and extend the reflected rays backward with dashed lines to find the image point.

diagram.caption: Two rays and equal angles are enough to find the image.

paras: When light passes from one transparent material into another, it changes speed, and that change of speed makes it change direction. This bending is called refraction. Light travels fastest in a vacuum and slower in water and glass. When light enters a denser material, like going from air into water, it slows down and bends toward the normal. When it leaves a denser material and goes back into a rarer one, it speeds up and bends away from the normal. If the ray enters exactly along the normal, straight on, it does not bend at all, although it still slows down.

The bent straw in a glass of water is the classic example. Light from the underwater part of the straw refracts as it leaves the water, bending away from the normal. Your eye follows the outgoing rays backward in a straight line, so the straw appears to be in a different place from where it really is, and it looks broken at the surface. A swimming pool looks shallower than it really is for the same reason: the light from the bottom bends as it leaves the water, and your brain places the bottom higher than it is. Never judge the depth of water by looking at it, because refraction always makes it look shallower.

To draw a refraction diagram, draw the boundary between the two materials as a straight line and the normal at right angles to it. Draw the incident ray in the first material with an arrowhead pointing toward the boundary. At the boundary, draw the refracted ray in the second material: toward the normal if the light is entering a denser material, away from the normal if it is entering a rarer material. Label the angle of incidence in the first material and the angle of refraction in the second material, both measured from the normal.

A glass block shows refraction twice: once when the light enters the glass, bending toward the normal, and once when it leaves, bending away from the normal. The ray that comes out is parallel to the ray that went in, but shifted sideways. This sideways shift is called lateral displacement, and it grows with the thickness of the block. You can observe it safely at home with a glass of water and a pencil: look at the pencil from the side and then move your head, and the apparent shift changes with the viewing angle. Drawing the two bends on paper makes the shift obvious and easy to explain in an exam.

diagram.alt: Reflection vs Refraction at a Glance
diagram.caption: One bounces back, the other passes through and bends.

sections.h2: Total Internal Reflection and Everyday Uses
paras: When light travels inside a denser material toward a rarer one, and the angle of incidence is large enough, the light does not leave at all: it reflects back inside. This is called total internal reflection. It happens only when light goes from denser to rarer, and only beyond a certain critical angle. Diamonds sparkle because their shape makes light reflect internally many times before it escapes. Fibre-optic cables carry internet and phone signals as pulses of light bouncing inside a thin glass fibre by total internal reflection, with almost no loss over long distances.

Mirages are another example. On a hot day, the air just above a road is hotter and rarer than the air above it. Light from the sky bends as it passes through layers of air of different density, and at a large enough angle it reflects totally, so you see a shimmering patch that looks like water. It is not water; it is the sky, reflected by hot air. Rainbows are different: they form when sunlight refracts as it enters a raindrop, reflects once inside the drop, and refracts again as it leaves, splitting white light into colours. The same splitting happens in a glass prism, because different colours bend by different amounts.

You can ask it to explain why a pool looks shallower than it is, or to quiz you on reflection versus refraction. points: Light travels in straight lines; angles in optics are measured from the normal.
Law of reflection: angle of incidence equals angle of reflection.
A plane mirror gives an upright, same-size, virtual, laterally inverted image.
Refraction is bending caused by a change of speed when light enters a new material.
Total internal reflection happens when light in a denser material hits the boundary beyond the critical angle.

faqs.q: Why does a straw in water look bent?
faqs.a: Light from the underwater part of the straw bends away from the normal as it leaves the water. Your eye follows the outgoing rays backward in a straight line, so the straw appears in a different position above the surface, and it looks broken at the water line.

faqs.q: What is a virtual image?
faqs.a: A virtual image is one where the light rays only appear to meet. In a plane mirror, the rays do not actually meet behind the mirror; your brain follows the reflected rays backward and sees the image there. A virtual image cannot be caught on a screen.

faqs.q: Why does a pool look shallower than it really is?
faqs.a: Because of refraction. Light from the bottom bends away from the normal as it leaves the water, and your brain places the bottom higher than its true position. Never judge water depth by looking at it.

faqs.q: Does light bend when it enters glass straight on?
faqs.a: No. A ray that enters along the normal, at zero angle of incidence, does not change direction, although it slows down. Bending happens only when the ray enters at an angle.

faqs.q: What is total internal reflection used for?
faqs.a: It is used in fibre-optic cables, which carry signals as light bouncing inside thin glass fibres, and it explains the sparkle of a diamond and the mirage on a hot road.

title: Sound Waves and Echo: Vibration, Frequency and Echo
desc: Vibration, frequency, and echo are linked to musical instruments and empty halls so pupils can hear the physics in daily life.
intro:
Every sound you have ever heard began with something vibrating. A drum skin vibrates, a guitar string vibrates, your vocal cords vibrate, and the vibrations travel through the air to your ears as sound waves. Sound needs a material to travel through, which is why there is no sound in the vacuum of space. Understanding sound means understanding three ideas: vibration makes the sound, frequency decides the pitch, and the way sound bounces back gives us echoes.

This article follows sound from its source to your ear. You will learn how a vibrating object pushes air into waves, why a short string gives a high note and a long string gives a low one, what an echo is and how it can be used to measure distance, and why an empty hall sounds so different from a furnished room. Along the way you will meet musical instruments and empty halls, two places where the physics of sound is easy to hear. Keep the ideas tied to sounds you know, and the definitions will stay with you far longer than memorised lines. Class material is listed on the [books page](/books.html), with solved notes on the [solved notes page](/solved.html) and more articles on the [blog index](/blog/).

paras: A sound source is always vibrating. Touch a drum after it is struck and you can feel the skin trembling. Pluck a rubber band stretched over an empty box and you can see it blur with vibration while you hear its note. Speak while touching your throat and you can feel your vocal cords vibrating. The vibration pushes the air next to it, squeezing the air into compressions, regions where the air particles are close together, and then letting it spread into rarefactions, regions where the particles are farther apart. These compressions and rarefactions travel outward as a longitudinal wave, in which the air particles vibrate back and forth in the same direction as the wave travels.

Because sound is a wave in a material, it cannot travel through a vacuum. The famous classroom demonstration places a ringing bell inside a jar and pumps the air out: as the air leaves, the sound fades away, even though the bell keeps vibrating. Sound travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids, and slowest in gases, because the particles in solids are packed tightly and pass vibrations on quickly. In air at ordinary temperatures, sound travels at about 340 metres per second, which is why you see lightning before you hear the thunder: the light reaches you almost instantly, but the sound takes seconds to cover the same distance.

Frequency is the number of vibrations per second, measured in hertz (Hz). It decides the pitch of a sound: a high frequency gives a high-pitched sound, and a low frequency gives a low-pitched sound. A short, tight guitar string vibrates faster and gives a higher note than a long, loose string. A child's voice is usually higher pitched than an adult's because the vocal cords are shorter and vibrate faster. Human hearing covers roughly 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz; sounds below that range are called infrasound and sounds above it ultrasound. Dogs can hear some ultrasound that humans cannot, which is why a dog whistle is silent to us.

Loudness is different from pitch. Loudness depends on amplitude, the size of the vibration. A drum hit hard vibrates with a large amplitude and sounds loud; the same drum tapped gently vibrates with a small amplitude and sounds soft. The two ideas are independent: a sound can be high and soft, like a distant whistle, or low and loud, like a nearby drum. Pupils often mix them up, so learn them as a pair: frequency controls pitch, amplitude controls loudness. When a question mentions a bigger vibration, it is talking about amplitude and loudness; when it mentions faster vibration, it is talking about frequency and pitch.

diagram.caption: Vibration, frequency, amplitude, and wave: one map for the whole topic.

sections.h2: Musical Instruments: Sound You Can See
paras: Musical instruments are physics laboratories that you can hear. In a string instrument, like a guitar or a harmonium string, the pitch is controlled by three things: length, tension, and thickness. A shorter string gives a higher note, a tighter string gives a higher note, and a thinner string gives a higher note. Guitar players press a string against a fret to shorten the vibrating part and raise the pitch. A sitar or violin player does the same by choosing where to press or pluck.

In wind instruments, like a flute or a bansuri, the vibrating air column inside the tube makes the sound. Covering a hole lengthens the vibrating column and lowers the note; uncovering a hole shortens it and raises the note. In a drum or tabla, the skin vibrates, and the size and tension of the skin set the pitch. Try this safely at home: stretch rubber bands of different thicknesses over an empty box and pluck them. The thick band gives a low note and the thin band a high note, and pressing a band in the middle shortens it and raises the note. You have just reproduced the physics of every string instrument with a box and three rubber bands.

An echo is the reflection of sound. When sound hits a hard, smooth surface like a wall, a cliff, or the far side of a valley, it bounces back, and if it returns after at least about one tenth of a second, your ear hears it as a separate sound: an echo. If the reflection returns too quickly, it blends with the original sound and you hear a prolonging, not an echo. That is why a small room does not give a clear echo, but a large empty hall or a mountainside does.

Echoes can measure distance, because sound travels at a known speed. If you clap in front of a distant wall and the echo returns after 2 seconds, the sound has travelled to the wall and back in 2 seconds, so the one-way time is 1 second and the distance is speed times time, about 340 metres. Bats use the same idea with ultrasound: they send out squeaks, listen for the echoes, and build a picture of obstacles and insects in the dark. Ships use sonar the same way underwater to find the depth of the sea or the location of a school of fish. The formula to remember is simple: distance equals speed times time, divided by two when the time is for the round trip.

diagram.caption: One clap, one echo, and the speed of sound give the distance.

paras: Walk into an empty hall and clap: the sound lingers, bouncing from wall to wall. Walk into the same hall filled with people, carpets, and curtains, and the clap dies quickly. The difference is absorption. Hard, smooth surfaces reflect sound well, so the sound keeps bouncing and you hear reverberation, the lingering of sound after the source stops. Soft, rough materials absorb sound, converting its energy into a tiny amount of heat, so the sound dies away.

This is why prayer halls, classrooms, and auditoriums are designed with sound in mind. Too much reverberation makes speech unclear, because each word's echo overlaps the next word. Too much absorption makes a room feel dead and a speaker hard to hear at the back. Curtains, carpets, and the bodies of an audience all absorb sound, which is why a hall sounds different when it is full. Engineers use sound-absorbing panels on walls and ceilings to tune a room. A classroom with bare walls and a tin roof will be noisy and echoey; adding a soft board, curtains, and bookshelves absorbs reflections and makes the teacher's voice clearer. Noise pollution is the same physics at town scale: traffic, horns, and loudspeakers are unwanted sound, and walls, trees, and distance all reduce it.

points: Every sound begins with a vibrating source; sound waves are compressions and rarefactions in a material.
Frequency in hertz decides pitch; amplitude decides loudness.
Sound cannot travel through a vacuum and moves at about 340 m/s in air.
An echo is reflected sound; it can measure distance using speed times time, halved for the round trip.
Hard surfaces reflect sound and cause reverberation; soft materials absorb it.

faqs.q: Why do we see lightning before we hear thunder?
faqs.a: Light travels at about 300,000 km/s and reaches you almost instantly, while sound in air travels at about 340 m/s. Over a distance of a few kilometres, the sound takes several seconds to arrive, so you see the flash first.

faqs.q: What is the difference between frequency and amplitude?
faqs.a: Frequency is the number of vibrations per second, measured in hertz, and it decides pitch. Amplitude is the size of the vibration, and it decides loudness. A sound can be high and soft or low and loud, because the two are independent.

faqs.q: How far away is a wall if the echo returns after 2 seconds?
faqs.a: The sound travelled to the wall and back in 2 seconds, so the one-way time is 1 second. Distance = 340 m/s x 1 s = 340 metres. Always halve the round-trip time before multiplying.

faqs.q: Why does an empty hall echo more than a full one?
faqs.a: Hard, bare walls reflect sound, so it keeps bouncing and lingers as reverberation. People, carpets, and curtains absorb sound, so in a full hall the reflections die away quickly and speech is clearer.

faqs.q: Can sound travel through space?
faqs.a: No. Sound needs a material, solid, liquid, or gas, to carry its vibrations. Space is a vacuum with no material, so a vibrating object there makes no sound that can reach anyone.

title: Electricity Basics: Current, Voltage and Resistance
desc: A water-pipe analogy makes current, voltage, and resistance intuitive, so pupils can read circuits instead of fearing them.
intro:
Electricity runs your home, your school, and your phone, yet it is invisible, which makes it feel mysterious. The good news is that electric circuits follow a simple analogy: think of electricity like water flowing through pipes. Current is like the flow of water, voltage is like the pressure that pushes the water, and resistance is like a narrow pipe that holds the flow back. Once that picture is in your head, circuits stop being mysterious and start being readable.

This article introduces the three quantities one at a time, shows how they are measured, and brings them together in Ohm's law, the single most useful relationship in school electricity. You will learn what a volt, an ampere, and an ohm actually mean, why a bulb glows, why wires get hot, and how to stay safe around electricity. By the end you will be able to look at a simple circuit diagram, name what each part does, and predict what happens when you change the battery or the bulb. Related safe circuit work is covered in [electric circuits and safe experiments](/blog/science-electric-circuits-safe-experiments.html). More class material is on the [books page](/books.html) and the [blog index](/blog/).

paras: Imagine a water tank on a roof connected by a pipe to a tap at ground level. The height of the tank gives the water pressure: a higher tank pushes the water harder. The rate at which water flows out of the tap is like the current. A narrow or clogged pipe resists the flow, so less water comes out, just as a thin wire or a bulb resists electric current. A wide, clear pipe lets water rush through, just as a thick, short wire lets current flow easily.

Now translate the picture to electricity. The battery is the tank: it provides the push. The wires are the pipes: they carry the flow. The bulb is a narrow section of pipe, or a water wheel: it resists the flow and uses the energy to do something, in this case to glow. The switch is the tap: open it and the flow stops, close it and the flow starts. Every circuit question can be checked against this picture. If the question asks what happens when the battery is stronger, think of a taller tank. If it asks what happens when the wire is thinner, think of a narrower pipe.

diagram.caption: One analogy, three quantities: push, flow, and opposition.

paras: Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge, measured in amperes (A). In a metal wire, the charge is carried by electrons, tiny negatively charged particles that drift through the metal. When the circuit is complete, electrons flow from one terminal of the battery, through the wires and the bulb, and back to the other terminal. Conventional current is drawn in diagrams as flowing from the positive terminal to the negative terminal, which is the opposite direction to the electron flow, but for circuit calculations the conventional direction is the one used.

Current is measured with an ammeter, which is connected in series, in the path of the current, so that the current flows through it. The symbol for current is I, and one ampere is one coulomb of charge passing a point every second. A torch bulb may draw a fraction of an ampere, while a room heater draws many amperes. The bigger the current, the more charge flows per second, and the more energy is delivered to the device. If a wire is cut or a switch is open, the circuit is broken and no current flows at all, however strong the battery is.

sections.h2: Voltage: The Push That Drives Current
paras: Voltage is the energy given to each unit of charge, measured in volts (V). It is the push that drives the current around the circuit. A 1.5 V cell gives each coulomb of charge 1.5 joules of energy; two cells in series give 3 V and push the charge with twice the energy. Voltage is measured with a voltmeter, which is connected in parallel, across the component, so that it compares the energy at the two ends of the component.

A common confusion is to think that voltage is used up like fuel. It is better to think of voltage as a difference in energy between two points. As charge flows through a bulb, it loses energy to the bulb, which glows and warms, so the voltage across the bulb drops. The battery then gives the charge energy again. In a series circuit, the voltages across the components add up to the battery voltage. In a parallel circuit, each branch gets the full battery voltage, which is why the bulbs in your home are wired in parallel: each one gets the full mains voltage and can be switched independently.

Resistance is the opposition to the flow of current, measured in ohms (symbol: the Greek letter omega). Every component resists current a little, and some resist a lot. A bulb's filament has high resistance, so it gets hot and glows when current passes through it. A copper connecting wire has low resistance, so it carries current without heating much. Resistance depends on the material, the length, and the thickness of the conductor: longer wires resist more, thicker wires resist less, and some materials, like copper, resist far less than others, like nichrome.

A resistor is a component made to provide a chosen resistance, and a variable resistor or rheostat lets you change the resistance and so control the current. Dimmer switches and fan regulators work this way: more resistance means less current and a dimmer bulb or a slower fan. Insulators, like plastic and rubber, have such high resistance that almost no current flows through them, which is why plugs and wire coverings are made of plastic. Conductors, like copper and aluminium, have low resistance and carry current easily.

sections.h2: Ohm's Law and Reading a Circuit
paras: Ohm's law ties the three quantities together: V = I x R, voltage equals current times resistance. If you know any two, you can find the third. A bulb with a resistance of 10 ohms connected to a 3 V battery draws a current of 0.3 A, because I = V / R = 3 / 10. If you double the voltage with the same resistance, the current doubles. If you double the resistance with the same voltage, the current halves. Learn the triangle trick: cover the quantity you want, and the remaining two show the formula. Cover V and you see I x R; cover I and you see V / R; cover R and you see V / I.

To read a circuit diagram, trace the loop from the battery's positive terminal, through each component, back to the negative terminal. Ask three questions: is the loop complete? Where is the push, the battery or cells? Where is the resistance, the bulb or resistor? In a series circuit there is one path, so the same current flows everywhere, and adding a bulb dims all of them because the total resistance rises. In a parallel circuit there are branches, so each branch gets the full voltage and can be switched separately. When a question asks you to predict a change, change one quantity in your mind, hold the others steady, and use Ohm's law to find the result. That is the whole method, and it works for every school circuit question.

diagram.caption: Find the two quantities you know, then use the triangle.

paras: Electricity is useful and dangerous, so learn the safety rules as part of the physics. Never touch a switch, plug, or wire with wet hands, because water lowers the resistance of your skin and lets more current flow through you. Never poke anything into a socket, and never use a device with a damaged wire or a cracked plug. If someone receives an electric shock, do not touch them directly while they are still in contact with the source: switch off the power first, then get an adult and medical help.

At home, fuses and circuit breakers protect the wiring. If too much current flows, the fuse melts or the breaker trips and breaks the circuit before the wires overheat and cause a fire. That is why you must never replace a fuse with a thicker wire: the protection disappears. For school experiments, use only low-voltage batteries, never mains electricity, and work only with your teacher's permission and supervision. Electricity deserves respect, not fear: the same rules that keep you safe also explain why the safety devices exist, and they are worth learning as carefully as any formula.

You can ask it to explain series versus parallel circuits using the bulbs in your own home.
